summary: 20/p fails (no 5-divisible 4/p solution) at 60 primes 5<p≤1e5 (63 incl. 2,3,5; last 90001), confirmed. 33/60 failures are p≡1 (mod 5) vs 25% base; 21/60 are p≡1 (mod 120) vs ~3% base: 21 of 286 such primes (7.3%) fail, vs 39 of ~9300 others (0.4%). Strong local fingerprint at 5 and 2/3.
next: Test whether the p≡1 (mod 120) enrichment is a character-sum effect for 20/p (predict failure density by (5/p),(2/p),(3/p)) and extend 20/p to 1e6 on p≡1 (mod 120) only.

summary: Composite n≤4000, m=5..48: 1556 composite failures; every one has a prime q|n with m/q failing (0 exceptions). Converse false: 137775 composite (m,n) have a failing prime divisor but only 1556 fail (e.g. 7/4 solvable, 7/2 fails). Failure is inherited from some prime divisor, not from all.
next: Test 'all prime divisors solvable ⇒ composite solvable' for m≤13 up to n≤1e5 (any counterexample would be a real finding); then look for the proof.

summary: FF engine (scripts/bs_ff_es.py, Q=5): for constant numerator 4 there are ZERO solutions for every monic P of degree 3 and 4, since lc(4X−P)=3 ∉{1,2} (engine lc condition); constants 1,2,3 give 159240, 41070, 5000 (deg 3 total). Sign/non-square twist A=2T vs A=T: total #ES over monic P deg3 16450 vs 4110 (x4.0), deg4 416223 vs 82350 (x5.1). So the non-square twist cuts counts ~4–5× and the FF analogue of 4/n (constant numerator 4) is degenerate by the lc lemma.
next: Check whether the lc lemma already in EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD.md covers constant numerators c with c−1 ∉{1,2}; if not, the FF '4/P' analogue should use a numerator with lc∈{2,3} (e.g. A=2 or 3) and be compared with the ℤ-side fingerprint.

summary: Numerator-4 FF analogue is zero (see Z0355), so only A=T/2T were used. P≡1 on all of F_5 needs deg P ≥5; the unique deg-5 monic such P gives #ES=22 for A=T and 0 for A=2T (n=1, too small to test a 2521 analogue).
next: Enumerate P≡1 mod all irreducibles of degree ≤2 (deg ≥ 11) with A=T for a sample, to see if the count is larger than for random P of the same degree.

summary: Monic irreducible P over F_5 (deg 2,3,4; 10,40,150 polys): mean #ES(T,P) = 5.4, 25.6, 56.8; mean #ES(2T,P) = 1.6, 4.0, 6.2; the ratio T/2T grows 3.4 → 6.4 → 9.2 with degree. The twist effect grows with degree, a sign that the 'colour at ∞' interacts with the Euler-product normalisation.
next: Extend to deg 5–6 (q=5) and test whether the ratio tends to (q-1)/… or grows like q^{deg/2}; then compare with the Euler-product prediction of EXSET/FF notes.

summary: Pseudosquare-type P (P(c) a nonzero square in F_5 for every c∈F_5, monic deg 5, 32 polys): mean #ES(T,P)=659 vs 2361 for 200 random monic deg-5 P (A=T). A local square condition at all degree-1 primes cuts the solution mean by ~3.6×, a Lehmer-style effect on the FF side.
next: Measure the same statistic at deg 6–7 and split by the residue pattern (χ(P(c))) to see whether the reduction is multiplicative over c.

summary: Independent brute force (exists x≤y≤z; two_term completion; scripts/z52b_p1_U01_twoterm.py) reproduces the raw failure sets for m=8,12,16,20 at all 165 primes 5<p≤1000: 0 mismatches. Bundling/OEIS submission itself not done (not a Pass-1 mathematical step).

Variant counter run for m=5 and m=8 on primes ≤1e5 (data/z52b/pass1/U01/var_m{5,8}_pr1e5.txt): U matches raw m5 data for all 9592 rows. Shape V7 (x=y or y=z) is zero exactly for p≡1 (mod 5) (2387 primes, 0 exceptions), which is the isosceles law of Z0973 confirmed independently.

Not run in this pass. Smallest meaningful test: count (x,y,z) with 1/x+1/y−1/z=4/p, z ≤ p², for p ≤ 2e4 — needs a new counter (divisor method over z, two-term completion), about 1–2 h of coding plus a run.
next: Write the z-capped signed counter (C) and fit log count vs log² p.

summary: Last failures p≤1e5: 8/p 241, 12/p 12241, 16/p 83449, 20/p 90001, 24/p 97777; 20/p and 24/p are censored at the window top, so the fit is not possible yet. Single-n timing of the counter: 0.84 s at 1e6, 10.6 s at 1e7, 125 s at 1e8.

summary: Timed the full counter on single primes: 0.84 s at 1e6, 10.6 s at 1e7, 125 s at 1e8 (≈n^1.07). Extrapolated to n=119 945 383 009 ≈ 2–3 CPU-days single-core with the current code; needs the shift cap / 128-bit path of the item.
next: Implement the capped 128-bit variant, check against the 1e8 run, then one run.

summary: Greedy first term x = ⌈p/4⌉ completes to a two-term remainder (4x−p)/(px) for most primes ≤3000 (428/428 found within the window); lag x−⌈p/4⌉ has median 0, mean 0.09, max 5 at p=2521 and p=1201 (the ES-hard primes), then 3 at p=2689. The two hardest greedy primes are exactly the hard ES primes.
next: Run up to 1e6 (two-term test is cheap) and test whether lag ≥ 3 concentrates on the top-30 hard primes; if so, the greedy lag is a usable hardness proxy.

summary: 4-term reps of 4/p with x1≤x2≤x3≤x4 (x1 ∈[p/4,2p], x2 ≤4p), primes p≤100: 4696 sets total, 1371 with a mergeable pair (1/a+1/b unit). Each mergeable pair gives a 3-term rep, and each 3-term rep splits into a mergeable 4-term rep (1/c = 1/(c+1)+1/(c(c+1))), so the 4→3 merge carries exactly the ES content (no new handle).
Same computation as Z3073 (p≤100): mergeable 4-term reps exist for every prime tested; equivalence to 3-term ES is exact (split/merge), so the merging step is ES itself.

4-term reps of 4/p (p≤100): 4696 sets vs only a handful of 3-term x1 values per prime (e.g. p=37: 155 vs 6). Four terms are abundant; the loss in the 4→3 step is exactly the merge condition (same as Z3073).
ES over ℤ[1/2] (x,y,z ∈ ℤ[1/2]_{>0}) is the ℤ[1/S] case; the repo already proves ℤ[1/S]-ES is trivial for every S≠∅ (H06 batch, Z2037).

Multiplicative variant (1+1/x)(1+1/y)(1+1/z)=(p+4)/p with 2≤x≤y≤z, x,y ≤2p: no solution for 397 of the first 400 primes (≤2000). Caveat: bounded search; z is determined by x,y, so unbounded x,y is not excluded.
next: Redo with x,y up to p² to see whether the failure is a search-bound artefact.

summary: Relaxation 4/p = (a+b+2)/(ab−1) + 1/c with a,b ∈[2,2p] holds for all 299 primes ≤2000 (c unit fraction). So this sub-family of the 3×3 relaxation is not constraining at this scale.

Additive energy of reciprocals of 1..q/4 mod q vs integer interval energy: ratio 0.450 (q=101), 0.385 (q=503), 0.381 (q=1009). Only the two-fold energy is measured; three-fold and the sum-set side not checked.
M(p)∩[1,48] = {m: U_m(p)>0} over primes ≤1e5: residues of m mod 4 are uniform (0.248, 0.251, 0.250, 0.251). No mod-4 AP structure in M(p).

Binary digits vs residual log(U4+1) (p≤3e4): bit1 (= p mod 4 = 3) corr 0.66, popcount 0.34, bit2 0.39, bit3 0.11. The dominant signal is p≡3 (mod 4), i.e. the isosceles law for 4/p (Z0973); no extra Sierpiński-type signal checked beyond that.

Lower bound n_m ≥ exp(m^{1/3+o(1)}) for prime-numerator-type failures is proved in arXiv:2511.16817 (already in the repo: BRAINSTORM/z52_lit_es_direct.md). Our raw failure counts for prime m (m=5..47) grow with log-log slope ≈3.0, consistent but not a test of the bound.

Joint failure of 8/p and 12/p over primes 3<p<=1e5: empty (8/p fails at {11,17,131,241}, 12/p at 20 primes, disjoint). Independence predicts ~0.001 joint failures, so no structure either way.
Union check: for all primes 3<p<=1e5 at least one of 8/p, 12/p has a solution (disjoint failure sets). Consistent with the union conjecture in range; no certificate-line structure examined.
Composite-n failures for m≤13, n≤4000 are exactly 4 (11/4), 14 (13/14), 25 (12/25) — matches the item. Inheritance lemma not proved; see Z0746 for the composite test.
Confirmed: 7/p fails only at p=2 for primes ≤1e5, and 7/n fails only at n=2 for n≤4000. Hardest-7 vs hardest-4 comparison not run.

Divisibility monotonicity: for every nontrivial pair (m, mk), m,mk≤48, p≤1e5 with F(m)≠∅: F(m) ⊆ F(mk) holds 39/39 (e.g. F(8)={2,3,11,17,131,241} ⊆ F(16)); the reverse inclusion fails. 54/54 pairs in total if trivial ones counted.
next: Check whether F(m)⊆F(mk) holds up to 1e6 for m|mk with m ∈{4,8,12} and try to prove 'solvable mk/p ⇒ solvable m/p' for a sub-case.

summary: Hardness H(p)=#{m≤48: m/p fails} regressed on Legendre symbols (q/p), q≤30, plus p mod 8 and p mod 9 indicators over 9589 primes: R²=0.014. No quadratic-character structure.
10/n, 11/n, 13/n failure sets at small n reproduce the item exactly ({2,3,7,11,43,61,67,181}; {2,3,4,37}; {2,3,4,5,7,14,53,61,67,79,211,281}); already in the repo fingerprint notes.
15/p fails at 25 primes ≤1e5 incl. 4201, 12601, 20521 (confirmed). Enrichment of p≡1 (mod 120): 3 of 25 vs base rate 3% — no enrichment.

Failure counts (p≤1e5, incl. 2,3) for m=5..48 reproduce the item's sequence exactly (0,0,1,6,4,8,3,22,10,9,25,38,17,49,16,63,...). Regression log(#fail+1) ~ 2.83·log m + 0.71·[4|m] + 0.28·[3|m] + 0.26·[5|m], R²=0.974: growth law only.

Pairwise Spearman-type check: median correlation of log(1+U_m(p)) across primes ≤1e5 for m=5..48 is 0.27; this is dominated by the common size factor (log p). Clustering of numerators by residual profile not run.
Primes failing ≥15 numerators (m=5..48, p≤1e5): 39 primes, largest 421 — consistent with 'all < 700' within the window.
Primes ≤1e5 failing ≥2 numerators (m=5..48): 1103; 861 of 946 numerator pairs share a failure prime. Overlaps are dominated by hard primes; no local reason per exception attempted.

p−1 practical correlates with ES hardness: mean residual of log(U4+1) (quadratic in log p) is −0.31 for practical p−1 vs +0.17 otherwise (p≤3e4, 3242 primes); 0 of the top-30 hardest primes have practical p−1 (null ≈0.65^30). Effect persists within p mod 8 and mod 24 classes (−0.08 to −0.41).
next: Test whether the effect is a divisor-count effect of p−1 (compare with random n of same ω/Ω and same largest prime factor) and whether hard primes have p−1 with a large prime factor > the practical bound.

summary: U4(p) vs U4((p+3)/4) over 271 primes ≤3e4 with (p+3)/4 prime: raw Spearman 0.657 (matches item). Residual correlation after removing a quadratic in log p is still 0.50 — the size confound does not explain it.
next: Partial out p mod 8 and the 2-adic class of (p+3)/4; compare with a null of random prime pairs (p, q) of similar size to check it is not generic.

summary: Isosceles (two equal denominators) criterion for m/p, p∤m: exists iff m | p+1, m | p+2, or m | 2p+1 (elementary gcd case analysis; brute force verified for p≤200, m∈{4,5,7,8}). For m=4 this is the known p≡3 (mod 4) law. Generalisation only; no ES content.
